title: The first Gibson jazz party with Ralph Sutton and Teddy Wilson
summary: Gibson hires Ralph Sutton, Cutty Cutshall, Wild Bill Davison, Edmund Hall and Jack Lesberg plus Teddy Wilson's trio for an invitation-only Labor Day party, with the band traveling to Aspen by bus.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: Say, Cliff, we were just talking about the very great impressario and jazz promoter, Richard (Dick) Gibson and his great jazz parties which he gives every year around Labor Day out in Vail and Aspen, and California at the Broadmore Hotel. And you mentioned that when you was a young man, you used to come down to Condon's and listen to the great bands that they had at Condon's, and all of the guys that he liked -- you and Wild Bill Davis son and a bunch of guys, and you said he went back to Denver and decided to give a jazz party in honor of his dear wife, Mattie Gibson, and you said that Ralph Sutton was the lead piano player down there and then Schroeder Shrader Shroder was the regular pianist, but he had become sick and so Gibson decided to use some of his own friends, use some of you guys, all of his favorite bands from Condon's at his jazz party. What about that?

... the intermission piano player at Condon's for several years was Ralph Sutton, and he just loved Ralph. So he hired Ralph to be our piano player at that first party -- so that was the band. Ralph Sutton, Cutty Cutshall, Wild Bill Davis son, Edmund Hall, Jack Lesberg on bass. Then he hired one other group, which was Teddy Wilson's trio. And that's all the music he had. Teddy Wilson's trio ...
Who was in his trio? Can you remember? Could that drummer been Bert Dollinger, Cliff?
That was some trio, by the way -- he was a very fast drummer by the way.
Excellent musician. And I think he lives up there. He was also in to art. He came from Sweden and made his home in Aspen. He's there still.
And I think -- and I can't be positive, but I think it was Major Holly he put on bass.
It could well be. Or Gene Ramey.
I don't think Gene was up there.
Well, we'll roll along here. Anyway, that was his party. He had a very select -- I think he had 80 to 100 people.
This was Dick Gibson's first party?

Yes, his party which was a private party -- and we played all the songs that they wanted, and what we would do every Labor Day weekend, we went up there first, you spent the first night at his home and had a little jazz session there, private, and then I forget -- we first went up in a bus. And they had a fire in the back of the bus, they were cooking a great big ham to make sandwiches, and we all went up in a big motor bus because the band was small then, and
of course, his guests had to get up there by themselves -- it's quite a way from Denver, up to Aspen.
